newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols mixed; T-bonds vols up.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols mixed; T-bonds vols up.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. debt futures options were mixed in late-morning trade Wednesday as dealers anticipated gains in T-bond futures but said the Eurodollar futures market remained indecisive.
At 1130 CDT/1630 GMT, implied volatility for December T-bond options was up 0.10 percentage point at 10.25 percent, according to dealers at Chicago Board of Trade.
One CBOT dealer, with a major U.S. investment firm, said volatilities were creeping up as the market began eyeing the 112-00 area in futures.
"If we don't break through that, there's a good chance volatility will drift back down," he said. Meanwhile, it appears December T-bond futures are building a base, he said.
He also said some dealers were counting on a flight-to-quality reaction from the stock market.
"The Treasury market is a relatively cheap product to buy with a secure, cheap yield," he said, adding that some increased retail activity in bonds had already been seen.
Some Eurodollar options dealers agreed that the long end of the curve was undervalued, which could account for the slight increase in T-bond options volatilities.
Among the morning's larger trades were purchases of 2000 November 114-00 calls, 1000 December 112/116 call spreads, and 1000 113-00 calls by different investment houses.
"Those are all bullish trades and yesterday we had quite a number of bullish trades as well," a dealer said.
In contrast to T-bond options, implied volatilities for Eurdollar futures options were flat to slightly lower at Chicago Mercantile Exchange, dealers said.
Implied volatility for December Euro options was unchanged from Tuesday's U.S. settlement at 10.9 percent. March volatility was down 0.20 percentage point at 14.9 percent.
"Everything, especially in our market, is keyed into what the Fed is doing," one CME dealer said. "If volatility does pick up, it will be because you have an increasing difference of opinion."

Currently, the market has no clear opinion as to the Fed's monetary intentions. If opinion divides as it clarifies -- that is, if half the market decides the Fed is likely to tighten while the other half begins looking for an ease -- volatilities will spike higher, he said.

However, if the market remains neutral over the next few months, volatilities for longer dated Eurodollar options will begin to rise, he said. "Then you would have to believe that at least the middle of the Euro curve is undervalued."
Neither T-bond nor Eurodollar option dealers expected to see volatilities rise strongly ahead of Friday's U.S. producer price and retail sales data.
"There's no one number that's going to be a compelling reason for the Fed to make a decision yet," a dealer said.
